clauses.title: Structure of an Enterprise Risk Assessment
clauses.text: Banks should maintain a documented financial-crime risk assessment that identifies the main categories of inherent risk across the institution, including customers, products and services, geographies and delivery channels. The assessment should describe the methodology used, the data sources relied on, and the reasoning behind each rating. Senior management should review the results, and the board should receive a summary so that resources and controls can be aligned with the risks the bank actually faces.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · BSA/AML Risk Assessment · item 01

clauses.title: Assessing Customer Risk Factors
clauses.text: Banks should evaluate inherent risk arising from the customer base by grouping customers according to relevant characteristics rather than treating all relationships alike. Useful factors include ownership complexity, business type, expected transaction volumes, use of intermediaries, and the presence of politically exposed individuals. The bank should quantify how many relationships fall into higher-risk groups, explain why those groups were chosen, and revisit the groupings when the customer mix shifts materially.

clauses.title: Product and Service Inherent Risk Review
clauses.text: Banks should assess each product and service for features that could allow illicit funds to move quickly, anonymously or across borders. Relevant considerations include transfer speed, transaction limits, the ability to fund or withdraw through third parties, and the degree of customer anonymity. New products and significant feature changes should receive a documented risk review before launch, with expected controls identified and accepted by accountable management.

clauses.title: Geographic Exposure Analysis
clauses.text: Banks should analyse the geographic footprint of their customers, counterparties and transaction flows to understand where exposure to money laundering and sanctions risk is concentrated. The analysis should consider domestic areas designated as higher risk as well as foreign jurisdictions with weak controls, significant corruption, or elevated illicit activity. Banks should document the sources used to rate locations and update ratings when conditions or business activity change.

clauses.title: Delivery Channel and Third-Party Risk
clauses.text: Banks should consider how customers are onboarded and served when rating inherent risk. Non-face-to-face relationships, remote account opening, reliance on introducers, and outsourced service providers can weaken visibility into who is using the bank. Management should assess whether identity verification and monitoring remain effective through each channel, and should evaluate vendors supporting these activities before onboarding them and periodically thereafter.

clauses.title: Residual Risk and Assessment Updates
clauses.text: Banks should compare inherent risk ratings with the strength of their controls to reach a residual risk conclusion for each risk area. Where residual risk exceeds the bank's stated appetite, management should set remediation actions with owners and deadlines. The assessment should be refreshed on a regular cycle and also when events occur that change the risk profile, such as entering a new market, launching a product, or changing a key process.

clauses.title: Data Inputs and Quality for Risk Assessment
clauses.text: Banks should ensure that the data used to build a risk assessment is complete, accurate and traceable to its source systems. Examiners would expect management to identify the data elements behind each inherent-risk measure, document known gaps or manual adjustments, and test extracts for consistency before results are relied upon. Where data is unavailable for a business line, the bank should state the limitation openly and apply conservative assumptions rather than treating missing information as low risk.

clauses.title: Board and Senior Management Oversight of Results
clauses.text: Banks should present risk assessment results to the board and senior management in a form that supports informed decisions. Reporting should summarize the main inherent risks, the strength of related controls, the resulting residual ratings and any actions that remain open. Senior management should be accountable for approving the assessment, challenging unexpected conclusions, and tracking remediation to completion, while the board should receive enough detail to judge whether the bank operates within its stated risk appetite.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · BSA/AML Risk Assessment · item 08

clauses.title: Independent Validation of Scoring Methodology
clauses.text: Banks should subject the methodology used to score inherent risk and control effectiveness to periodic independent review. The reviewer should be free of day-to-day responsibility for the assessment and should evaluate whether factor weightings are reasoned, whether rating thresholds separate materially different risks, and whether results behave sensibly when inputs change. Findings should be reported to management, and the bank should record how each weakness in the methodology was addressed or why it was accepted.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · BSA/AML Risk Assessment · item 09

clauses.title: Linking Risk Assessment to Monitoring Calibration
clauses.text: Banks should use the conclusions of the risk assessment to shape how transaction monitoring and related detection activity are designed and tuned. Areas rated higher in risk should receive more granular scenarios, lower tolerance for unexplained activity and closer review of alerts, while lower-risk areas may justify simpler coverage. Management should be able to show how specific assessment findings led to specific monitoring changes and should reassess coverage when the assessment identifies a new typology or exposure.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · BSA/AML Risk Assessment · item 10

clauses.title: Documenting Rationale for Risk Ratings
clauses.text: Banks should keep clear written support for every rating assigned within the risk assessment. Documentation should explain which facts and data were considered, how judgment was applied where evidence was mixed, and who approved the final conclusion. A knowledgeable reader who was not involved in the exercise should be able to follow the reasoning from inherent exposure through control assessment to the residual result, and understand why the bank reached that rating.

clauses.title: Resource Allocation Aligned to Risk Priorities
clauses.text: Banks should align compliance staffing, technology investment and training effort with the priorities that emerge from the risk assessment. When the assessment shows rising exposure in a business line, management should consider whether investigators, analysts and systems are sufficient to manage it, and should document decisions to add or redeploy capacity. Shortfalls that cannot be closed quickly should be escalated, with interim compensating measures recorded and reviewed until resources are adequate.

clauses.title: Risk Assessment Triggers for Business Change
clauses.text: Banks should reassess their money laundering and terrorist financing risk profile whenever a significant business change occurs, rather than waiting for the next scheduled review. Launching a new product or feature, altering a core process, entering a new market, or adding a new customer segment can shift inherent risk and weaken existing controls. Management should evaluate the change before launch, record the expected effect on risk ratings, and confirm that monitoring, staffing, and training are adequate for the altered profile.

clauses.title: Aggregating Risk Across Business Lines
clauses.text: Banks should consolidate risk assessment results from individual business lines, affiliates, and branches into a coherent enterprise view so that concentrations and gaps are visible. Examiners expect management to look beyond isolated unit ratings and consider how the same customer, product, or counterparty may present exposure in several areas at once. The consolidation method should be consistent, reasonably transparent, and able to show why a combined rating differs from the ratings of its components.

clauses.title: Risk-Based Customer Profile at Onboarding
clauses.text: Banks should develop a customer profile at account opening that captures the nature and purpose of the relationship, expected activity, products requested, and the customer's occupation or business type. The profile should be sufficiently detailed to allow the bank to understand what normal activity looks like and to recognize departures from it. Information collected should be proportionate to the risk the customer presents and should be documented in a form that monitoring staff can readily use.

clauses.title: Beneficial Ownership Identification for Legal Entities
clauses.text: Banks should identify and take reasonable steps to verify the natural persons who own or control legal entity customers. Management should understand ownership layers, recognize structures that obscure control, and escalate cases where owners cannot be identified or where the stated structure lacks a plausible business rationale. Procedures should explain how ownership information is refreshed and how discrepancies found later in the relationship are resolved and recorded.

clauses.title: Enhanced Due Diligence for Higher-Risk Customers
clauses.text: Banks should apply enhanced due diligence to customers whose risk rating indicates greater exposure to money laundering or terrorist financing. Additional measures may include corroborating source of funds and source of wealth, understanding the expected counterparties, obtaining senior management approval to proceed, and performing more frequent reviews. The depth of inquiry should be commensurate with the risk and the rationale for conclusions should be retained in the customer file.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Customer Due Diligence · item 03

clauses.title: Ongoing Monitoring and Periodic Profile Refresh
clauses.text: Banks should conduct ongoing monitoring to maintain and update customer information and to identify and report suspicious transactions. Refresh cycles should follow customer risk, with higher-risk relationships reviewed more often, and should also be triggered by events such as unusual activity, adverse information, or a material change in ownership or business model. Monitoring results should feed back into the customer risk rating in a documented way.

clauses.title: Geographic Risk in Customer Risk Rating
clauses.text: Banks should consider geographic exposure when rating customers, including residence, place of incorporation, operating locations, and the destinations or origins of expected funds flows. Jurisdictions with weak anti-money laundering frameworks, heightened corruption, sanctions exposure, or significant illicit finance activity warrant greater scrutiny. Management should define how geographic factors are weighted, review the country list regularly, and ensure new corridors are assessed before activity begins.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Customer Due Diligence · item 05

clauses.title: Reliance on Third Parties for Due Diligence
clauses.text: Banks that use vendors or other third parties to collect or verify customer information should remain accountable for the quality of the resulting due diligence. Management should assess the provider's capabilities before engagement, define required data standards and escalation rules in writing, test outputs on a sample basis, and monitor service performance. Deficiencies should be remediated promptly, and the bank should be able to retrieve underlying records on request.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Customer Due Diligence · item 06

clauses.title: Politically Exposed Person Identification and Review
clauses.text: Banks should establish procedures to identify customers, beneficial owners and controlling persons who hold or have recently held prominent public functions, as well as their close family members and associates. Identification should occur at onboarding and again during periodic screening. Where a match is confirmed, banks should obtain information on source of wealth and source of funds, require senior management approval to establish or continue the relationship, and apply heightened monitoring proportionate to the exposure to corruption and misuse of public funds.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Customer Due Diligence · item 07

clauses.title: Governance and Validation of Customer Risk Rating Models
clauses.text: Banks should govern their customer risk rating methodology as a managed model. Management should document the factors used, the weight given to each, and the rationale for score thresholds. The methodology should be independently validated on a regular cycle and after material changes to products or customer populations. Validation should test whether ratings separate higher-risk from lower-risk customers in practice, and overrides of model output should be limited, justified in writing and reviewed by a second person.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Customer Due Diligence · item 08

clauses.title: Non-Face-to-Face Onboarding and Digital Identity Verification
clauses.text: Banks that open relationships remotely should recognise that the absence of in-person contact can raise inherent risk. Controls should include reliable document authentication, matching of the applicant to the presented identity, device and location consistency checks, and detection of synthetic or stolen identities. Banks should set out when a remote applicant must be routed to additional verification, and should review the performance of digital onboarding tools, including false acceptance rates, at regular intervals.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Customer Due Diligence · item 09

clauses.title: Event-Driven Reviews of Customer Due Diligence
clauses.text: In addition to scheduled refreshes, banks should define events that prompt an unscheduled review of a customer's due diligence file. Examples include a sudden change in transaction patterns, a change of ownership or control, adverse media, a law enforcement inquiry, or the filing of a suspicious activity report. The bank should set timeframes for completing these reviews, record the outcome, and update the risk rating and the expected activity profile where the findings warrant it.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Customer Due Diligence · item 10

clauses.title: Adverse Media and Public Information Screening
clauses.text: Banks should use reputable public information sources to identify negative news linked to customers, beneficial owners and key counterparties. Screening should be proportionate to risk, cover financial crime allegations as well as sanctions and regulatory actions, and be repeated during ongoing monitoring. Analysts should assess the credibility, relevance and age of each finding, document how it affected the customer's risk rating, and escalate serious or unresolved matters to a designated senior reviewer.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Customer Due Diligence · item 11

clauses.title: Handling Incomplete Due Diligence and Relationship Exit
clauses.text: Banks should define what happens when due diligence cannot be completed or when a customer declines to provide required information. Procedures should restrict new activity on the account, set a reasonable deadline for remediation, and require escalation to compliance staff. Where gaps remain unresolved, management should decide whether to exit the relationship and consider whether a suspicious activity referral is warranted. Each decision and its rationale should be recorded and available for examination.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Customer Due Diligence · item 12

clauses.title: Documentation of Due Diligence Decisions
clauses.text: Banks should document the information gathered during customer due diligence, the risk rating assigned, and the reasoning behind any decision to accept, escalate or decline a relationship. Records should be clear enough that an independent reviewer can understand why a conclusion was reached without asking the original analyst. Banks should keep these records accessible for the full relationship and for a reasonable period afterward, and should record who approved exceptions and why.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Customer Due Diligence · item 13

clauses.title: Consolidated Customer View Across Business Lines
clauses.text: Banks should maintain a consolidated view of each customer across products, business lines and affiliated entities, so that due diligence findings and risk ratings are not held in isolated systems. Where a customer holds several accounts or services, the bank should be able to see combined activity and apply the highest relevant risk consideration. Banks should define how due diligence information is shared internally and how conflicting ratings for the same customer are reconciled.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Customer Due Diligence · item 14

clauses.title: Due Diligence on Trusts and Holding Vehicles
clauses.text: Banks should apply additional care when the customer is a trust, personal holding company or other vehicle that can obscure who controls the assets. Expected practice is to understand the purpose of the structure, the source of the funds placed in it, and the roles of settlors, trustees and those who benefit or exercise effective control. Where the structure has no evident business or personal rationale, the bank should escalate the relationship for enhanced review before opening accounts.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Customer Due Diligence · item 15

clauses.title: Training and Quality Assurance for Due Diligence Staff
clauses.text: Banks should ensure that staff who collect and assess customer information are trained for their specific roles and understand how their work supports the risk rating. Training should be refreshed when products, customer segments or procedures change. Banks should also run a quality assurance program that samples completed files, measures error and rework rates, and reports recurring weaknesses to senior management so that corrective action is tracked through to closure.

clauses.title: Processor Onboarding Due Diligence
clauses.text: Banks should perform documented due diligence before opening an account for a third-party payment processor. Reviews should confirm the processor's legal structure, beneficial owners, management background, licensing status, business model and the types of payments it handles. Banks should also check for adverse media, regulatory actions and prior account closures at other institutions. The depth of review should match the risk the relationship presents, and the results should be retained and available to examiners.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Third-Party Payment Processors · item 01

clauses.title: Contract Terms Allocating Compliance Duties
clauses.text: Banks should document the processor relationship in a written agreement that sets out each party's compliance responsibilities. The agreement should require the processor to follow applicable financial-crime requirements, to disclose changes in its client base or activities, and to give the bank timely access to transaction records and underlying client information on request. It should also state the circumstances in which the bank may suspend processing, hold funds or end the relationship.

clauses.title: Monitoring Returns and Unauthorized Transaction Rates
clauses.text: Banks should track return rates, chargebacks and customer complaints associated with each processor relationship, and compare them with reasonable thresholds and peer norms. Unusually high or rising rates of returned or disputed items, particularly those marked unauthorized, may signal fraud or deceptive practices by the processor's clients. Banks should investigate the causes promptly, document the findings, and escalate results that remain unexplained to appropriate senior staff for a decision on next steps.

clauses.title: Verifying the Processor's Own Client Controls
clauses.text: Banks should understand how a processor screens and monitors the merchants or originators it serves, since the bank usually has no direct relationship with them. This includes reviewing the processor's client acceptance procedures, its ongoing monitoring methods and its handling of high-risk business types. Banks should obtain evidence that these controls operate as described, such as sample client files, and should use audit or independent testing rights to confirm them periodically.

clauses.title: Red Flags and Suspicious Activity Escalation
clauses.text: Banks should train staff to recognize warning signs in processor relationships and to escalate them for suspicious activity review. Examples include a processor that resists providing client information, routes payments through many unrelated accounts, uses frequent changes of client names, or shows activity inconsistent with its stated business. Escalation procedures should set clear timelines, assign responsibility for investigation, and ensure that decisions and supporting reasoning are recorded.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Third-Party Payment Processors · item 06

clauses.title: Periodic Relationship Review and Exit Decisions
clauses.text: Banks should review each processor relationship on a periodic, risk-based schedule and whenever its activities change materially. Reviews should re-examine the original due diligence, monitoring results, complaints and any control weaknesses found. Where risks cannot be adequately managed, banks should have a defined process for restricting services, requiring remediation or exiting the relationship in an orderly way, while continuing to meet reporting obligations throughout the wind-down.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Third-Party Payment Processors · item 07

clauses.title: Nested Processors and Layered Relationships
clauses.text: Banks should identify whether a payment processor routes items through other processors, resellers or sub-processors, and should understand each layer's role in the payment chain. Where nesting exists, the bank should obtain information on the downstream parties, confirm that the primary processor applies comparable oversight to them, and treat limited visibility into end originators as a factor that raises inherent risk and calls for tighter controls or restricted volumes.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Third-Party Payment Processors · item 08

clauses.title: Settlement Accounts and Funds Flow Transparency
clauses.text: Banks should map how funds move between the processor, its clients and the bank, including the structure of settlement, reserve and pooled accounts. Management should be able to trace activity to the underlying originators, understand when funds are released, and assess whether account structures could obscure beneficial ownership or the source of funds. Arrangements that limit the bank's ability to see individual originator activity should be escalated and justified before approval.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Third-Party Payment Processors · item 09

clauses.title: Management Information and Board Reporting
clauses.text: Banks should provide senior management and the board with regular, meaningful reporting on processor relationships. Reports should cover the number and size of relationships, concentration of volume, exceptions to policy, open findings, and material changes in risk profile. Reporting should be clear enough to support informed decisions about risk appetite, resource needs and whether specific relationships remain consistent with the bank's stated tolerance for financial crime risk.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Third-Party Payment Processors · item 10

clauses.title: Training for Relationship and Compliance Staff
clauses.text: Banks should ensure that staff who manage, approve or monitor processor relationships receive training suited to their roles. Training should address how processors operate, typical misuse patterns, the warning signs that distinguish higher-risk activity, and when and how to escalate concerns. Relationship managers should understand that commercial objectives do not override compliance obligations, and training content should be refreshed as products and typologies change.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Third-Party Payment Processors · item 11

clauses.title: Independent Testing of the Processor Program
clauses.text: Banks should subject their processor oversight program to periodic independent testing by qualified personnel who are not involved in day-to-day operations. Testing should evaluate whether onboarding, monitoring and escalation practices follow written procedures, whether risk ratings are supported, and whether identified weaknesses are tracked to closure. Results should be reported to senior management, and the scope should be adjusted when the bank's processor footprint grows.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Third-Party Payment Processors · item 12

clauses.title: Cross-Border Processor Exposure and Data Access
clauses.text: Banks should consider additional risk when a processor serves originators or beneficiaries in other countries, or stores relevant records abroad. Banks should confirm that transaction and client information can be obtained promptly on request, that local legal restrictions on data sharing are understood, and that monitoring reflects the higher-risk corridors involved. Exposure to jurisdictions with weak controls should prompt enhanced scrutiny or limits on activity.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Third-Party Payment Processors · item 13

clauses.title: Reserve Arrangements and Exposure Limits
clauses.text: Banks should establish reserve or collateral arrangements proportionate to the credit, fraud and return risk that a payment processor presents, and should set clear exposure limits on the volume and value of items the processor may submit. Reserve levels and limits should be reviewed whenever the processor's client mix, product scope or return experience changes materially. Banks should document the rationale for each setting and escalate requests for higher limits to senior risk management rather than approving them at the relationship level.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Third-Party Payment Processors · item 14

clauses.title: Remote Customer Onboarding and Identity Assurance
clauses.text: Banks that open accounts entirely through digital channels should apply identity verification measures proportionate to the absence of face-to-face contact. Controls should combine document authentication, data-source corroboration, and device and network signals, and should define when an application is escalated for manual review. Management should test how well these controls detect synthetic identities and altered documents, and should reassess them whenever the onboarding flow, data provider, or applicant population changes materially.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Electronic Banking · item 01

clauses.title: Authentication Strength and Account Takeover Monitoring
clauses.text: Banks should align the strength of customer authentication with the risk of the electronic services offered. Higher-risk activity, such as changing contact details, adding payees, or raising transfer limits, should require stronger or additional verification. Monitoring should look for signs of account takeover, including credential resets followed by rapid fund movement, unfamiliar devices, and abrupt changes in session behavior, and alerts should feed the suspicious activity review process.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Electronic Banking · item 02

clauses.title: Oversight of Third-Party Digital Service Providers
clauses.text: When a bank relies on a technology vendor, fintech partner, or processor to deliver electronic banking services, it remains responsible for the financial crime risk those services create. Banks should perform due diligence on the provider's compliance capabilities before onboarding, define in the agreement who monitors activity and who reports concerns, obtain access to relevant data, and review the provider's performance periodically against agreed expectations.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Electronic Banking · item 03

clauses.title: Monitoring Calibration for Real-Time Payments
clauses.text: Banks offering instant or near-instant electronic payments should recognize that reduced settlement time leaves little opportunity to recall funds after the fact. Monitoring should therefore include pre-transaction or in-flight checks suited to the speed of the service, with thresholds and scenarios calibrated to observed typologies such as rapid pass-through activity and mule account behavior. Management should validate these settings before launch and following significant volume growth.

clauses.title: Cross-Border Access to Electronic Banking Services
clauses.text: Because online and mobile services can be reached from almost anywhere, banks should assess the risk that customers or third parties access accounts from locations outside the markets the bank intends to serve. Controls should use location indicators, such as network address and device data, to identify access from higher-risk or unsupported locations, and should define restrictions, enhanced review, or reporting steps when such access is detected or when the bank expands into a new market.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Electronic Banking · item 05

clauses.title: Risk Assessment for Digital-Only Business Customers
clauses.text: Before extending electronic banking to a new category of business customers that will never visit a branch, banks should update their risk assessment to reflect how those customers transact. The assessment should consider expected payment volumes, ownership transparency, the nature of the business, and the ability to verify legitimacy remotely. Resulting expectations for ongoing due diligence and account activity profiles should be documented and approved by appropriate management.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Electronic Banking · item 06

clauses.title: Remote Deposit Capture Risk Controls
clauses.text: Banks offering remote deposit capture should assess the risk of the service before launch and whenever limits or eligible customers change. Expected controls include customer eligibility screening, deposit limits aligned to expected activity, detection of duplicate or altered item images, and review of unusual deposit patterns across accounts. Banks should also monitor for rapid movement of deposited funds to third parties and should document how exceptions are escalated for investigation.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Electronic Banking · item 07

clauses.title: Device and Session Intelligence for Linked Accounts
clauses.text: Banks should use device and session signals to help identify relationships between electronic banking accounts that would otherwise appear unconnected. Useful signals include shared device identifiers, repeated access from the same network, use of anonymizing tools, and automated session behavior. Management should define how these signals feed monitoring and investigations, test them for false positives, and ensure that linked-account findings are considered when reviewing customer risk ratings.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Electronic Banking · item 08

clauses.title: Governance of API and Data-Sharing Access
clauses.text: Banks that expose application programming interfaces or permit customer-authorized data sharing should govern that access as part of their financial crime risk program. Management should maintain an inventory of connected parties, define the data and functions each may use, require strong consent and credential handling, and monitor connection volumes and behavior for abuse. Banks should be able to suspend a connection promptly when misuse or control weaknesses are identified.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Electronic Banking · item 09

clauses.title: Detecting Mule Activity in Digital Accounts
clauses.text: Banks should design monitoring to detect money mule activity in accounts opened and operated entirely online. Indicators include newly opened accounts receiving numerous unrelated inbound payments, funds moved out shortly after arrival, activity inconsistent with stated purpose, and account details shared across applicants. Banks should combine onboarding data with transaction behavior, set clear escalation paths, and use confirmed cases to refine scenarios and customer education.

clauses.title: Assessing Inherent Risk in Funds Transfer Activity
clauses.text: Banks should assess the inherent risk of their funds transfer services by considering transaction volume, average and peak values, the speed of settlement, and the mix of domestic and cross-border flows. Services that permit high-value, same-day or irrevocable transfers generally carry greater exposure and warrant stronger preventive and detective controls. The assessment should be documented, refreshed when the service changes materially, and used to set monitoring intensity and staffing.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Funds Transfers · item 01

clauses.title: Payment Message Information Integrity
clauses.text: Banks should ensure that originator and beneficiary information is captured accurately at initiation and carried unchanged through each stage of the payment chain. Systems should reject or hold messages with missing, truncated or obviously meaningless party details, and staff should not strip or alter fields to speed processing. Management should periodically test message samples to confirm that required information remains complete and that exceptions are investigated and resolved promptly.

clauses.title: Cross-Border Corridor and Country Risk
clauses.text: Banks should evaluate the risk of each cross-border funds transfer corridor they support, considering the sanctions posture, corruption and secrecy levels, and the strength of anti-money laundering oversight in the counterparty country. Corridors with elevated risk should receive enhanced review of payment purpose, tighter monitoring thresholds, and senior approval before launch. The corridor assessment should be revisited whenever conditions in a destination or origin country change significantly.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Funds Transfers · item 03

clauses.title: Intermediary and Correspondent Payment Transparency
clauses.text: Banks that route transfers through correspondent or intermediary institutions should understand how those parties handle payment instructions and should expect full transparency of underlying party information, including in cover payment arrangements. Due diligence should address the intermediary's own controls and its downstream relationships. Where an intermediary cannot or will not pass through complete information, the bank should escalate, restrict the routing, or end the arrangement.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Funds Transfers · item 04

clauses.title: Monitoring for Pass-Through and Rapid Movement
clauses.text: Banks should monitor funds transfer activity for patterns inconsistent with a customer's expected profile, such as funds received and sent onward within a short period, repeated transfers just below internal review levels, or many unrelated counterparties sending to one account. Monitoring rules should be tuned using risk assessment results, alerts should be investigated by trained staff, and decisions about suspicious activity reporting should be recorded with clear rationale.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Funds Transfers · item 05

clauses.title: Controls over Digital and Third-Party Initiation
clauses.text: Banks should apply risk-based controls to channels through which customers or partners initiate transfers, including online banking, mobile applications, and programmatic connections offered through third-party providers. Expected controls include strong authentication, limits suited to the customer type, device and session anomaly checks, and contractual rights to obtain information from the provider. Management should reassess channel risk whenever a new initiation method or provider is introduced.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Funds Transfers · item 06

clauses.title: Funds Transfer Recordkeeping and Retrieval
clauses.text: Banks should keep complete records of funds transfers and be able to retrieve them promptly when requested by internal reviewers, auditors or authorities. Records should capture the originator, beneficiary, amounts, dates, instructions received and the institutions involved. Retention periods and storage formats should be defined by policy, protected from alteration, and tested regularly so that information remains accessible after system migrations, process changes or the onboarding of new payment processing providers.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Funds Transfers · item 07

clauses.title: Due Diligence on High-Volume Wire Customers
clauses.text: Banks should apply enhanced due diligence to customers whose business models involve frequent or high-value wire activity, such as trading firms, payment facilitators and import-export businesses. Diligence should establish the expected purpose, counterparties, volumes and geographies of payments, and should be refreshed when activity departs from that profile. Account opening for such customers should require approval from a senior reviewer who understands the related funds transfer risks.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Funds Transfers · item 08

clauses.title: Alert Investigation and Escalation Standards
clauses.text: Banks should maintain documented standards for investigating alerts generated on funds transfer activity. Investigators should review the customer profile, related accounts, counterparties and payment history, and record the reasoning behind each disposition. Alerts that remain unexplained should be escalated to a designated decision-maker within set timeframes. Management should track backlogs, ageing and quality assurance results, and should adjust staffing when investigative capacity does not keep pace with alert volumes.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Funds Transfers · item 09

clauses.title: Training for Payment Operations Personnel
clauses.text: Banks should provide role-specific training to staff who originate, review, release or repair funds transfers. Training should cover common typologies, red flags in payment instructions, the handling of manual overrides and the steps for escalating concerns. Content should be updated when products, systems or payment channels change, and completion should be tracked. Staff in high-risk roles should receive more frequent and practical instruction, including case-based exercises.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Funds Transfers · item 10

clauses.title: Handling of Returned, Recalled and Rejected Payments
clauses.text: Banks should control how returned, recalled, amended and rejected funds transfers are processed, since repeated reversals and redirections can indicate attempts to disguise the source or destination of funds. Procedures should require that funds be returned only to the original source, that changes to beneficiary details be independently verified, and that patterns of frequent reversals be reported to monitoring and investigation teams for review.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Funds Transfers · item 11

clauses.title: Independent Testing of Funds Transfer Controls
clauses.text: Banks should subject funds transfer controls to periodic independent testing by qualified personnel who are not involved in daily operations. Testing should evaluate whether monitoring scenarios, screening tools, approval limits and recordkeeping work as designed and cover the bank's actual risk exposure. Findings should be reported to senior management and the board, with remediation owners and deadlines, and follow-up confirming that corrective actions were effective.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Funds Transfers · item 12

clauses.title: Risk Assessment of Money Services Business Customers
clauses.text: Banks should assess the inherent risk of each money services business customer before and after account opening, rather than treating the whole category as uniformly high or low risk. Relevant factors include the range of services offered, transaction volumes and values, the customer base served, the maturity of the business, and the strength of its own compliance program. The resulting rating should drive the depth of due diligence and the intensity of monitoring applied.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Nonbank Financial Institutions / MSBs · item 01

clauses.title: Onboarding Due Diligence for Money Services Businesses
clauses.text: Banks should collect enough information at onboarding to understand who owns and controls a money services business and how it earns revenue. Expected practice includes confirming registration and any required state licensing, reviewing ownership and management, obtaining a description of services and customer types, and sighting the written compliance program. Where the prospective customer cannot or will not provide this information, the bank should decline the relationship or escalate the decision to senior compliance staff.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Nonbank Financial Institutions / MSBs · item 02

clauses.title: Service and Product Mix Risk Factors
clauses.text: Banks should evaluate how the specific services a money services business offers affect its exposure to illicit finance. Domestic money transmission, currency exchange, check cashing, and stored-value or prepaid issuance each present different speed, anonymity, and transaction-size characteristics. Banks should document which services the customer provides, note where product features such as higher load limits or anonymous use increase risk, and tailor expected controls to those features.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Nonbank Financial Institutions / MSBs · item 03

clauses.title: Cross-Border Corridor and Geographic Exposure
clauses.text: Banks should understand the countries and corridors through which a money services business sends or receives funds, and should weigh them in the customer's risk rating. Greater attention is warranted where flows involve jurisdictions with weak supervision, elevated corruption, sanctions exposure, or known conflict-related financing risks. Banks should ask for corridor-level volume information, compare it with the stated business profile, and reassess the rating when the corridor mix changes materially.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Nonbank Financial Institutions / MSBs · item 04

clauses.title: Ongoing Monitoring of Money Services Business Accounts
clauses.text: Banks should monitor money services business accounts against an expected activity profile set at onboarding and refreshed periodically. Monitoring should look for unexplained changes in volume, structuring patterns, rapid movement of funds in and out, unusual counterparties, and activity inconsistent with the stated customer base. Alerts should be reviewed by trained staff, decisions documented, and suspicious activity escalated promptly through the bank's established reporting process.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Nonbank Financial Institutions / MSBs · item 05

clauses.title: Evaluating the Customer's Compliance Program and Testing
clauses.text: Banks should form a view on the quality of a money services business customer's own anti-money-laundering program, since the bank relies on it to manage risk upstream. Reasonable steps include reviewing its policies, the designated compliance officer's role, staff training, and the results of independent testing. Material deficiencies or unresolved findings should prompt enhanced monitoring, remediation requests with deadlines, and, where necessary, a documented decision to restrict or close the account.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Nonbank Financial Institutions / MSBs · item 06

clauses.title: Pooled Account and Funds Commingling Transparency
clauses.text: Banks should understand how a money services business uses pooled or omnibus accounts to hold funds for its own customers. Banks should determine whether the business commingles customer funds with operating funds, whether it can identify the underlying originators and beneficiaries on request, and how it reconciles balances. Where transparency is limited, banks should apply tighter transaction limits, request supporting records more often, and escalate the relationship for senior review.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Nonbank Financial Institutions / MSBs · item 07

clauses.title: Virtual Currency and Digital Asset Exposure
clauses.text: Banks should assess whether a money services business customer exchanges, transmits, or custodies virtual currency, since such activity can raise anonymity and speed-of-movement concerns. Banks should expect the customer to show how it verifies users, screens wallet addresses, and monitors on-chain activity for links to illicit sources. Banks should document the expected volumes and counterparties and reassess the relationship whenever the customer adds a new digital asset service.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Nonbank Financial Institutions / MSBs · item 08

clauses.title: Sanctions Screening Across Payment Flows
clauses.text: Banks should confirm that money services business customers screen their own clients, counterparties, and payment messages against applicable sanctions lists before funds are released. Banks should also screen the customer's transactions that pass through the bank, and should review how the customer resolves potential matches, records its decisions, and reports blocked or rejected items. Weak screening logic or delayed list updates should prompt corrective action and closer oversight of the account.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Nonbank Financial Institutions / MSBs · item 09

clauses.title: Completeness of Originator and Beneficiary Information
clauses.text: Banks should expect money services businesses to capture and pass along complete originator and beneficiary information with the payments they send through the bank. Banks should test samples of payment messages for missing, truncated, or implausible fields, and should treat repeated gaps as a red flag. Where the customer relies on intermediaries, banks should confirm that the data remains intact through each handoff and can be produced promptly for investigators.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Nonbank Financial Institutions / MSBs · item 10

clauses.title: Suspicious Activity Escalation for MSB Relationships
clauses.text: Banks should maintain a clear path for escalating unusual activity in money services business accounts to investigators and senior management. Alerts should be reviewed against the customer's stated business profile, with attention to structuring patterns, rapid movement of funds, and third-party deposits. Banks should document the rationale for filing or not filing a report, and should decide at defined intervals whether continuing the relationship remains within risk appetite.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Nonbank Financial Institutions / MSBs · item 11

clauses.title: Account Exit Decisions and Risk-Based Retention
clauses.text: Banks should make decisions to retain or exit money services business relationships through a documented, risk-based process rather than by blanket categorization. Each decision should weigh the customer's demonstrated controls, the bank's ability to manage the residual risk, and the quality of the customer's cooperation. Banks should record the reasons for an exit, coordinate timing with relevant control functions, and report exit trends to governance committees.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Nonbank Financial Institutions / MSBs · item 12

clauses.title: Risk Assessment of Foreign Correspondent Relationships
clauses.text: Banks should assess the inherent risk of each foreign correspondent relationship before opening the account and refresh that assessment as the relationship changes. The assessment should weigh the respondent's customer base, the products and services it will use, the countries where it operates, and the channels through which it submits activity. Banks should document the rating rationale and align the depth of due diligence and monitoring with the resulting risk level.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Foreign Correspondent Accounts (summary) · item 01

clauses.title: Due Diligence on Respondent Institutions
clauses.text: Banks should perform due diligence that establishes who owns and manages each respondent institution, how it is licensed and supervised in its home country, and what the respondent's own financial-crime program looks like. Reviewers should consider the respondent's reputation, past enforcement history, and the quality of its policies. Banks should keep the resulting file current and ensure that senior approval precedes activation of the relationship.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Foreign Correspondent Accounts (summary) · item 02

clauses.title: Nested Accounts and Downstream Clearing Exposure
clauses.text: Banks should identify whether a respondent offers its own services to other foreign financial institutions through the correspondent account, a practice often called nesting or downstream clearing. Where it does, banks should understand who those downstream parties are, what activity they conduct, and how the respondent screens them. Banks should restrict or decline relationships in which the respondent cannot provide meaningful transparency about these underlying users.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Foreign Correspondent Accounts (summary) · item 03

clauses.title: Ongoing Monitoring of Correspondent Transaction Flows
clauses.text: Banks should monitor correspondent activity on an ongoing basis, comparing actual wire and payment flows with the expected profile recorded at onboarding. Monitoring should look for unusual volumes, rapid movement of funds, repeated round-value payments, and activity involving unrelated third parties or unexpected countries. Scenarios and thresholds should be calibrated to the respondent's risk rating, and alerts should be investigated and resolved within set timeframes.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Foreign Correspondent Accounts (summary) · item 04

clauses.title: Enhanced Scrutiny for Higher-Risk Jurisdictions and Shell Banks
clauses.text: Banks should apply enhanced scrutiny to respondents located in or routing activity through jurisdictions with weak financial-crime controls, high corruption, or limited supervisory transparency. Additional measures may include site visits, independent reviews of the respondent's controls, and tighter transaction limits. Banks should not maintain relationships with shell banks and should confirm that respondents do not offer accounts to such entities.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Foreign Correspondent Accounts (summary) · item 05

clauses.title: Escalation, Information Requests, and Relationship Exit
clauses.text: Banks should maintain a clear process for escalating concerns about a foreign correspondent, including timely requests for information to the respondent about specific transactions or customers. Responses that are late, incomplete, or evasive should be reviewed by senior compliance staff. Where risks cannot be mitigated, banks should restrict services or exit the relationship in an orderly manner and retain records supporting the decision.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Foreign Correspondent Accounts (summary) · item 06

clauses.title: Payable-Through Account Controls and Sub-Account Holder Visibility
clauses.text: Banks should apply specific safeguards when offering payable-through arrangements that allow a respondent's own customers to transact directly through the bank's account. Management should understand who may draw on the account, confirm that the respondent performs comparable identification of those sub-account holders, and obtain identifying information on request. Banks should set limits on activity volume and permitted uses, test the respondent's controls periodically, and restrict or close the arrangement when transparency into underlying users is inadequate.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Foreign Correspondent Accounts (summary) · item 07

clauses.title: Governance, Training, and Independent Testing of Correspondent Programs
clauses.text: Banks should ensure that the program for foreign correspondent activity is supported by clear governance, including defined ownership, board or senior management reporting, and adequate staffing. Personnel who open, review, or approve respondent relationships should receive role-specific training on typologies and red flags. Banks should subject the program to periodic independent testing, track remediation of findings to completion, and update procedures when products, vendors, or respondent profiles change materially.
clauses.ref: FFIEC synthetic stand-in · Foreign Correspondent Accounts (summary) · item 08

clauses.title: Screening customers and owners at onboarding
clauses.text: Banks should screen every prospective customer, and the beneficial owners, controllers and authorised signatories associated with that customer, against applicable sanctions lists before an account or product is opened. Screening should also consider ownership structures in which blocked persons hold a significant combined interest, even where no single listed party is a named owner. Where screening cannot be completed, the relationship should not proceed until the open questions are resolved and documented.

clauses.title: Alert review and escalation discipline
clauses.text: Banks should maintain written procedures for reviewing potential sanctions matches so that each alert is assessed consistently, promptly and by suitably trained staff. Reviewers should record the reasoning behind every disposition, including the identifiers compared and the evidence relied upon. Alerts that cannot be confidently discounted should be escalated to a designated sanctions specialist, and transactions should be held while that escalation is pending. Management should monitor alert ageing and backlog levels to make sure delays do not weaken the control.

clauses.title: Calibration and testing of screening tools
clauses.text: Banks should calibrate name-matching logic, fuzzy thresholds and transliteration handling to the risks of their own business, and should test that calibration before deployment and at regular intervals afterwards. Testing should use representative samples of known true matches and realistic variations to show that relevant hits are not missed. Changes to rules, data feeds or screening software, including those supplied by third parties, should be approved, validated and documented, with results reported to senior compliance management.

clauses.title: Blocking, rejecting and record retention
clauses.text: Banks should have clear procedures for the action to take once a true sanctions match is confirmed, including whether the property must be blocked or the transaction rejected. Procedures should identify who may authorise the action, how affected funds are held and how required reports to the authority are prepared and submitted on time. Banks should retain the supporting records of each confirmed match and its resolution in a form that can be retrieved promptly for supervisory review.

clauses.title: Sanctions exposure review for new markets
clauses.text: Before entering a new country, region or corridor, banks should assess how comprehensive and targeted sanctions programmes affect the proposed activity. The assessment should consider local counterparties, intermediaries, transit routes and the likelihood that customers may have links to restricted territories. Where the exposure cannot be managed with existing controls, the bank should add geographic screening rules, restrict permitted activity or decline to proceed, and should record the rationale for its decision.
clauses.ref: OFAC synthetic stand-in · Screening obligations · item 1.6

clauses.title: Distinguishing blocking lists from sectoral lists
clauses.text: Banks should ensure that their screening programmes clearly distinguish between lists that require assets to be blocked and lists that impose narrower, activity-based restrictions. Procedures should explain how a match against each list type is handled, including whether the relationship must be frozen, the transaction rejected, or the activity permitted under conditions. Staff should be trained to recognise the difference, and escalation paths should reflect the different legal consequences of each outcome.

clauses.title: Ownership aggregation for blocked persons
clauses.text: Banks should design screening and due diligence so that entities owned in the aggregate by one or more listed persons are identified, even when the entity itself does not appear on any list. Institutions should collect ownership information sufficient to apply the relevant ownership threshold, consider combined holdings of several listed parties, and document how indirect ownership chains are assessed. Unresolved ownership questions should be escalated before an account is opened or a payment is released.

clauses.title: Handling sectoral list restrictions on debt and equity
clauses.text: Banks should establish controls for sectoral lists that restrict specific dealings, such as new debt beyond a stated maturity or new equity in named entities, rather than prohibiting all dealings. Screening hits against such entities should route to specialist reviewers who can assess the instrument, tenor and counterparties involved. Banks should record the rationale for each permitted or declined transaction and ensure product teams understand which features trigger a restriction.

clauses.text: Banks should ensure that changes to sanctions lists are reflected in screening systems promptly and that the update process is monitored for failures. Where a third-party vendor supplies list data or screening technology, the bank should verify completeness, test that new entries are ingested correctly, and retain accountability for results. Following each update, institutions should consider rescreening existing customers and in-flight transactions against the newly added names.

clauses.title: Aggregating Ownership Across Blocked Persons
clauses.text: Banks should recognise that an entity may be treated as blocked when one or more sanctioned persons own, in the aggregate, half or more of it, even if no single owner reaches that level. Screening procedures should therefore add together the direct and indirect interests of all listed owners in a customer or counterparty, and should not rely on reviewing each owner in isolation. Where aggregate ownership cannot be determined, the bank should treat the uncertainty as a risk requiring escalation.

clauses.title: Collecting Ownership Data at Onboarding
clauses.text: Banks should gather enough ownership information at onboarding to support meaningful sanctions screening of entity customers. This includes the names and percentage holdings of owners above a defined threshold, plus intermediate holding companies in the chain. The bank should set the threshold below the level that triggers aggregation concerns, verify the information against reliable documents, and record where information was unavailable, so reviewers understand the limits of any screening result.

clauses.title: Looking Through Layered Ownership Structures
clauses.text: Banks should look through layered ownership structures, such as holding companies, trusts and nominee arrangements, to find sanctioned persons who hold interests indirectly. Where an intermediate entity is majority-owned by a sanctioned person, that entity's own holdings should be attributed to that person in full. Banks should also treat unexplained complexity, opaque jurisdictions and inconsistent ownership records as warning signs. They should seek clarification before establishing or continuing the relationship.

clauses.title: Rescreening After List and Ownership Changes
clauses.text: Banks should rescreen their customer base promptly when sanctions lists are updated and whenever ownership information on an entity changes. Rescreening should cover related entities that may now meet the ownership threshold, not just names that appear on the list. Alerts should be reviewed and dispositioned within defined timeframes, with the rationale documented. Confirmed matches should be escalated immediately so that blocking or rejection steps and required reporting can be carried out.

clauses.title: Why Changes Trigger Risk Reassessment
clauses.text: Banks should reassess their financial-crime risk profile whenever a meaningful change alters who they serve, what they offer, where they operate or how they deliver services. A program that was sound when designed can become inadequate if new activity introduces exposures that existing controls were never built to address. Reassessment should therefore be treated as a standing part of change management, not an occasional exercise, so that control design keeps pace with the institution's actual risk.

clauses.title: Scoping the Assessment to the Change
clauses.text: Banks should scope each risk assessment in proportion to the nature and scale of the proposed change. A minor adjustment to an existing workflow may need only a short review of affected controls, while a new product line or a new customer population may call for a full analysis of inherent risk, control effectiveness and residual exposure. Banks should document why a given depth of review was chosen so that reviewers can later understand the reasoning behind it.

clauses.title: Evidence Used to Inform the Assessment
clauses.text: Banks should base their risk assessments on a range of credible evidence rather than on assumption alone. Useful inputs include internal transaction patterns, past suspicious activity reporting trends, findings from audits and testing, and national-level threat priorities published by authorities. Banks should record which sources were consulted, note any gaps in the available data, and explain how those limits affect confidence in the conclusions reached about the proposed change.

clauses.title: Assessing Third-Party and Delivery Channel Risk
clauses.text: Banks should consider how a change in delivery method or reliance on an outside provider affects their exposure. When a vendor will perform or support monitoring, onboarding or payment activity, the assessment should examine the provider's controls, the data it will handle and the bank's ability to oversee it. Accountability for compliance remains with the bank, so outsourcing should never be treated as a transfer of responsibility for identified risks.

clauses.title: Acting on Assessment Results and Review
clauses.text: Banks should ensure that assessment outcomes lead to concrete action. Where residual risk exceeds the institution's stated appetite, management should require additional controls, limit the scope of the change, or defer launch until gaps are closed. Results should be escalated to appropriate senior oversight, tracked to completion, and revisited after implementation to confirm that the controls operate as expected and that the original conclusions remain valid.

clauses.title: Assess Financial Crime Risk Before Launching Products
clauses.text: Banks should assess the financial crime risk of a new product or a material feature change before it is offered to customers. The assessment should consider how the product could be used to move value, hide ownership, or layer transactions, and should identify the controls needed to manage that exposure. Launch approval should depend on those controls being designed, resourced, and ready to operate, rather than being added after problems appear.

clauses.title: Reassess Risk When Entering New Markets
clauses.text: Banks should reassess their risk profile when they begin serving a new market or a new geographic area, whether directly or through counterparties. The review should weigh local illicit finance threats, the strength of oversight in that place, and the typical payment flows involved. Where the new exposure exceeds what current monitoring and screening can handle, the bank should strengthen those controls before activity begins and record the reasoning behind its decision.

clauses.title: Evaluate New Customer Types Before Onboarding
clauses.text: Banks should evaluate the risks of any new customer type or segment before onboarding begins at scale. Examples include customers with complex ownership, unfamiliar business models, or unusual expected transaction patterns. The evaluation should determine whether existing due diligence questions, risk ratings, and expected-activity baselines remain suitable, and should adjust them where the new population behaves differently from the customers the program was originally built around.

clauses.title: Review Process and Vendor Changes for Control Impact
clauses.text: Banks should review changes to operating processes, delivery channels, and third-party providers for their effect on the financial crime program. A new workflow, system, or outsourced service can weaken detection, create gaps in customer information, or shift accountability unclearly. The bank should test whether controls still work as intended after the change, confirm who is responsible for them, and keep evidence that the review took place and was approved.

clauses.text: Banks should record every condition attached to the approval of a new product or feature, assign each condition a named owner and a target completion date, and confirm closure with evidence. Open conditions should be reported to senior risk committees at regular intervals. Where a condition cannot be met on time, the bank should document the reason, apply interim controls, and reassess whether the original approval remains appropriate.

clauses.text: Banks should not treat vendor due diligence as complete at the point of onboarding. After approval, the bank should refresh its review of the provider when the scope of services expands, when ownership or key subcontractors change, or when performance and control findings suggest elevated exposure. Follow-up reviews should test whether the provider still meets the conditions set at approval and should be documented and retained for supervisory examination.

clauses.text: When a bank approves service to a new customer segment, it should schedule a follow-up review of early account activity against the expected profile recorded during due diligence. Material deviations in volumes, counterparties or funding sources should prompt enhanced scrutiny and, where needed, tighter limits or revised onboarding criteria. Findings should be shared with the business line and compliance so that segment assumptions are corrected promptly.

clauses.text: Banks that expand into a new geography should plan a structured post-approval assessment of the risks identified during due diligence. The assessment should examine whether local conditions, transaction patterns and available data sources match earlier assumptions, and whether required controls are operating effectively. Where gaps emerge, the bank should restrict further expansion until remediation is verified and the responsible oversight body has reviewed the outcome.

clauses.text: Banks should record every condition attached to the approval of a new product, feature or activity in a single approval file. Each condition should state its purpose, a named accountable owner, a completion deadline and the evidence that will show it has been met. Conditions that are vague or have no owner tend to lapse unnoticed, so approvers should decline to close an approval until the conditions are specific enough to be tested later.

clauses.text: Banks should schedule a follow-up review after an approved change goes live, rather than treating approval as the end of oversight. The review should compare actual customer mix, transaction volumes, alert levels and control performance with what was assumed at approval. Where results differ meaningfully from those assumptions, the bank should document the reasons, adjust controls as needed, and report the outcome to the committee that granted the original approval.

clauses.text: Banks should escalate promptly when a condition of approval is missed or when the approved activity changes materially after launch, for example through a new vendor, a wider customer base or an added geography. Escalation should go to the original approving body, which may extend a deadline, require added controls, limit activity or withdraw approval. Decisions and their rationale should be recorded so that supervisors and internal audit can trace them.

clauses.text: Banks should continue to oversee a newly engaged service provider once it begins performing activities for the bank. Oversight should include periodic review of service-level results, control testing outcomes, complaint and incident trends, and the provider's handling of customer due diligence tasks. Deficiencies should be documented, remediated within agreed timeframes, and considered when deciding whether to renew, restrict or terminate the relationship.

clauses.text: Banks should define measurable indicators that show when the risk profile of an approved activity has moved materially from what was assessed at approval, such as growth in volume, new customer types, or exposure to additional countries. clauses.title: Enhanced Measures for Call-for-Action Jurisdictions
clauses.text: Banks should apply enhanced due diligence to customers, counterparties and transactions with a meaningful connection to any jurisdiction that an international standard-setter has placed under a call for action. Institutions should refresh geography risk ratings promptly when a listing changes, re-flag affected relationships, obtain senior management approval before establishing or continuing higher-risk ties, and scrutinise the source of funds, the purpose of activity and the ultimate beneficial owners. Where risks cannot be mitigated, banks should consider restricting or exiting the relationship.

clauses.text: Banks should treat a jurisdiction that an international standard-setter has placed under increased monitoring as a heightened geographic risk factor, without applying a blanket refusal of business. When a country is newly flagged, banks should promptly re-assess affected customers, products and payment corridors, record the rationale for any change in risk rating, and calibrate monitoring thresholds and review frequency in proportion to the exposure. Banks should also confirm that the published deficiencies are reflected in their own risk assessment and that staff receive timely guidance on expected escalation.

clauses.text: The bank shall prohibit a payout agent from delegating any part of its contracted activity to a sub-agent or affiliate unless the bank has approved the arrangement in writing in advance. Any approved sub-agent shall be subject to the same due diligence, screening and contractual obligations as the primary agent, and the primary agent shall remain fully accountable to the bank for the conduct and controls of every party it uses.

clauses.title: Ongoing Monitoring of Agent Performance
clauses.text: The bank shall monitor each payout agent throughout the relationship using defined risk indicators. Indicators shall include volumes compared with expected profiles, rates of unusual activity reports, screening alert handling times, complaint patterns and findings from reviews. Results shall be reported to the responsible governance committee at least quarterly, and agents breaching agreed thresholds shall be placed on a remediation plan with assigned owners and deadlines.

clauses.title: Agent Staff Training and Annual Attestation
clauses.text: The bank shall require each payout agent to train all relevant staff on financial crime obligations before they handle bank-related activity and at least once every year thereafter. Training shall cover recognising suspicious behaviour, sanctions awareness and escalation routes. Each agent shall provide training records and an annual written attestation signed by a senior officer, and the bank shall treat missing evidence as a control breach requiring follow-up.

clauses.title: Suspension and Exit of Payout Agents
clauses.text: The bank shall maintain a documented procedure for suspending and terminating payout agents whose conduct or controls present unacceptable financial crime risk. Triggers shall include sanctions exposure, repeated reporting failures, obstruction of reviews and adverse regulatory findings. On exit, the bank shall preserve records, settle open items under supervision, assess whether regulatory reporting is required, and record lessons learned for future agent selection.

clauses.title: Verifying agent identity and legal existence
clauses.text: The bank shall verify the identity and legal existence of every agent before any agreement is signed or any activity is permitted. For corporate agents, the bank shall obtain certified formation documents, confirm the registered address and good standing with an independent source, and record the nature of the agent's business. Individual agents shall be verified against unexpired government-issued identification. No agent shall be activated on the basis of self-declared information alone, and any unresolved discrepancy shall be escalated to the relationship owner and compliance.

clauses.title: Beneficial ownership and control of agents
clauses.text: The bank shall identify and verify the natural persons who own or control each agent entity, including anyone holding a significant ownership share and at least one individual who exercises senior management control. Where ownership runs through holding companies, trusts or nominee arrangements, the bank shall trace the structure to its ultimate individuals. If the structure cannot be understood or evidenced to the bank's satisfaction, the agent shall not be onboarded, and the decision and its rationale shall be recorded.

clauses.title: Screening agents and their principals
clauses.text: The bank shall screen each agent, its beneficial owners, directors and key personnel against sanctions lists, politically exposed person data and adverse media before onboarding and on an ongoing basis thereafter. Potential matches shall be reviewed by trained analysts and resolved within defined timeframes, with the outcome documented. Where a confirmed sanctions match arises, the bank shall immediately suspend all dealings with the agent and follow the escalation path set by the financial crime compliance function.

clauses.title: Assessing agent risk by location and model
clauses.text: The bank shall assign each agent a risk rating that reflects the countries in which it operates, the customer types it introduces, the products it supports and the way it interacts with customers. Agents based in or serving higher-risk locations, or using remote-only introduction models, shall receive enhanced due diligence, including senior compliance approval and a documented review of expected activity volumes. The rating methodology shall be approved by compliance and reviewed at least annually.

clauses.title: Periodic and event-driven agent reviews
clauses.text: The bank shall refresh agent due diligence on a schedule set by risk rating, with higher-risk agents reviewed more frequently than lower-risk ones. Reviews shall also be triggered by events such as a change of ownership, adverse media, unusual referral patterns, regulatory action against the agent, or a material expansion of its services. Each review shall confirm that documents remain current, that screening is up to date and that the risk rating is still appropriate, with results retained in the agent file.

clauses.title: Agent accountability and exit for KYC failures
clauses.text: The bank shall require every agent to contractually commit to the bank's customer identification standards, to complete initial and annual training, and to cooperate with audits and information requests. Where an agent repeatedly submits incomplete or inaccurate customer information, or refuses to remediate findings, the bank shall restrict its permissions and may terminate the relationship. Terminations for financial crime concerns shall be reported to compliance so that suspicious activity reporting obligations can be assessed.

clauses.title: Audit and inspection rights in vendor contracts
clauses.text: The bank shall include in every vendor contract that supports a financial-crime control a right for the bank to audit, inspect and test the vendor's relevant systems, records and personnel. Audit rights shall be exercisable on reasonable notice, and without notice where the bank has reason to suspect a control failure. The vendor shall give auditors timely access and shall remediate findings within the period the bank sets. The bank shall retain the right to share audit results with its supervisors.

clauses.title: Supervisory cooperation and information requests
clauses.text: The bank shall require each vendor to cooperate with supervisory authorities that have oversight of the bank. Contracts shall oblige the vendor to answer information requests promptly, to produce documents in a usable format, and to make knowledgeable staff available for interviews. The vendor shall not withhold information on the grounds of commercial confidentiality where the bank needs it to meet a supervisory request. The bank shall set response deadlines in the contract and track compliance with them.

clauses.title: Restrictions on subcontracting and onward delegation
clauses.text: The bank shall prohibit a vendor from subcontracting or delegating any financial-crime control activity without the bank's prior written approval. Where approval is given, the contract shall bind the subcontractor to the same obligations on screening, monitoring, record keeping and reporting that apply to the vendor. The vendor shall remain fully accountable for the subcontractor's performance and shall disclose any change in the subcontracting chain before it takes effect. The bank shall reassess risk whenever the chain changes.

clauses.title: Escalation of suspicious activity by vendors
clauses.text: The bank shall require each vendor that handles customer activity to escalate suspicious or unusual activity to the bank's financial-crime unit within a defined period stated in the contract. The vendor shall record the facts observed, preserve supporting evidence and refrain from informing the customer or any third party of the escalation. Contracts shall name the responsible contacts on both sides and require the vendor to confirm in writing that its staff have been trained on these duties each year.
